headline: Two Russian missiles fell on Poland. Nobody was hurt.
summary: Two Russian missiles and a likely drone came down in Poland on Friday, one about 22 miles from where European troops were drilling for a postwar mission in Ukraine. No reports of injuries or damage. Poland's prime minister called it an intentional provocation. NATO's chief called it a grave violation of airspace. Moscow has not commented.

cover_question.q: Is this how a bigger war starts?

cover_answer: Not from this. A war needs all 32 NATO countries to agree.
table_question: If one friend gets hit, does the whole group have to fight back?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: Russia is fighting a war with its neighbor Ukraine. On Friday two of its missiles flew too far and came down in Poland, the country next door, one of them in a forest. It's like a ball thrown so hard it lands in the neighbor's yard. Nobody was hurt, and the grown-ups who run Poland are already on it.
5-7.why: Safe or not is the only question at this age. The neighbor's yard answers it.
5-7.why_long: A seven-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, and a missile in a forest an ocean away is not. The ball in the neighbor’s yard gives them one picture to hold, and ‘nobody was hurt’ is the sentence they came for. They read your face before your words, so say it plainly. Expect ‘could one land here?’ No. The war is across an ocean.

8-12.script: Russia fired over 110 missiles and 400 drones at Ukraine overnight. Two kept going and came down in Poland, 22 miles from European soldiers in training. Poland is in NATO: 32 countries sworn to defend each other, a buddy system with rules. All 32 must agree before anyone fights.
8-12.why: Fired, overshot, landed, club rules. It ends in a meeting.
8-12.why_long: A twelve-year-old is building chains of cause and effect, so the script lays one out: Russia fired, two missiles landed in Poland, Poland is in a club. The buddy system is the mechanism. The vote explains a meeting instead of a counterattack. Expect ‘that’s not fair, they got hit.’ Agree. The rule keeps 32 countries out of a war.

13-17.script: Is this how a bigger war starts? Article 5 says an attack on one NATO member is an attack on all 32, but only if all 32 agree it was one. Poland's prime minister calls it intentional. Britain's intelligence chief says Russia doesn't want war and fears a miscalculation. Who decides which this was?
13-17.why: Deliberate, and not wanting war, can both be true. Who decides?
13-17.why_long: A sixteen-year-old can hold two true things at once: the missiles were probably deliberate, and Russia probably does not want war with NATO. The script hands them both and asks who decides, Kuhn’s point that argument is practised on real cases. Expect ‘so Article 5 is a bluff?’ No: a promise with a vote attached, by design.

5-7.a: No. Nobody was hurt and nothing got broken. Grown-ups are checking where it fell.

8-12.q: Why did Russia shoot at Poland?
8-12.a: Russia hasn't said. Poland's leader thinks it was on purpose.

8-12.q: Is Poland going to fight back?
8-12.a: Not alone. Poland is in NATO. 32 countries decide together.

13-17.q: Is this how a bigger war starts?
13-17.a: Only if all 32 NATO members vote that it was an attack.

13-17.q: Why would Russia do it on purpose?
13-17.a: Tusk says the drills. A UK general fears a blunder more than a plan.
